turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr. Ellison, good afternoon. Have a seat. Before I go through the numbers, tell me what brought you in today.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, Doctor. I came in because your office called to say my blood thinner level was high, and I have been bruising rather easily.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm sorry to cut in. I'm Dana, I stay with him and I cook. He's been a little...
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. We'll get to that in a moment, Dana. Mr. Ellison, how long have you noticed the bruises?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, about four days, Doctor. They are on both arms. They do not hurt.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also had a nosebleed yesterday morning. It only lasted a few minutes, then it stopped.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is quite right. It stopped by itself, so I did not telephone anyone.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any fever this past week?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I have not had a fever.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. I have been breathing comfortably.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that changed?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I may have lost a pound or two, but I cannot be certain. My clothes fit just the same, and the bathroom scale jumps around.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. The INR I have in front of me today is 3.9. For the atrial fibrillation we aim for 2 to 3, so this is above range.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I have taken the warfarin every evening without fail, five milligrams. The fibrillation was diagnosed six years ago.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Urgent care put him on ciprofloxacin Friday, 500 milligrams twice a day, for a bladder infection. He has three days of it left. I wasn't sure if I should have...
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): You were right to keep it going. Ciprofloxacin can raise the INR. Has his green vegetable intake changed at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat whatever is served, Doctor. I would not know how to...
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I stopped the spinach and the kale about a week ago. He used to have a salad most days. I read that leafy greens clash with warfarin, so I cut them out.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): That helps me. Less vitamin K, plus the antibiotic, would push the INR up. What other medicines are you taking?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I take Metformine, five hundred milligrams with breakfast, for the sugar. Omprazole in the morning for heartburn. And Mizartan for the blood pressure, though I am afraid I cannot recall the strength.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. We will not change those today. Any blood in the urine, or black stools?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. The urine is clear, and the stools look normal to me.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He has seemed more tired this week. He still walks out to the mailbox, though.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): A little weary, yes, Doctor, but nothing I would call severe. I still read after dinner.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your arms. I see several small bruises on the forearms, no large hematoma, and your gums are not bleeding just now.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-two over seventy-eight. Pulse is 84 and irregular, which fits the atrial fibrillation.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, to summarise back. You are on warfarin five milligrams each evening for atrial fibrillation, today's INR is 3.9, ciprofloxacin was started for the bladder infection, and the leafy greens were stopped about a week ago. Those last two explain the high reading.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Starting tomorrow, take warfarin 4 milligrams by mouth each evening instead of the five, and skip tonight's dose. Keep taking the ciprofloxacin until it is finished. Please go back to a steady portion of spinach or salad, not a sudden large plate.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Four milligrams from tomorrow, and nothing tonight. I shall do exactly that. I appreciate you explaining it so carefully.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the bruising does not settle over the next week, we might arrange an ultrasound, though I do not need one today. I am booking your INR recheck in one week, and we will revisit the dose then. If you get a heavy nosebleed or black stool before that, come straight in.

spec.situation: Older patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation; INR result read aloud; antibiotic started elsewhere; green leafy diet changes; dose adjusted and recheck in a week.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
